newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Time Warner to slim down after Turner merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Time Warner to slim down after Turner merger.

text.p: Time Warner Inc. took control Thursday of Turner Broadcasting System Inc., paying $6.7 billion to reclaim the title of the world's biggest media group and promising to slim down quickly.

Executives of the combined company, including Turner Broadcasting founder Ted Turner, have been privately telling institutional investors that cost cuts will be coming and Time Warner's flamboyant spending history ended.

Time Warner Chairman Gerald Levin said Wednesday that planned cost-cutting would save the combined company some $600 million a year, according to people who attended a meeting with investors. The company is also believed to have hired consultants McKinsey & Co. to scour Time Warner for savings.
A Time Warner spokesman declined to comment.

Time Warner was also expected to resurrect efforts to pull back from owning and operating cable television systems, a capital-intensive business that accounts for much of the company's $17.5 billion in debt.
Turner, who will be vice chairman of Time Warner and the company's largest individual shareholder, told the investors meeting Wednesday that he wants the company's debt halved.
His remarks prompted speculation that Time Warner, the second-largest U.S. operator of cable TV systems, will spin off at least some of those operations.

Time Warner is a partner with U S West Media in many cable operations and is likely to seek a restructuring of that alliance, executives and analysts have said. U S West Media sued Time Warner when it announced its acquisition of Turner, but a Delaware judge earlier this year ruled against U S West.

"Everyone's on the same page on this," said Gordon Crawford, a fund manager at Capital Research Group, a major shareholder in both Time Warner and Turner Broadcasting. "Nobody wants $17 billion to $19 billion in debts at the end of the day."

Debt payments that have resulted in year after year of net losses have long overshadowed Time Warner's exceptionally strong operating performance, keepings its stock price down, Wall Street analysts say.
Some cuts already have been announced at Turner Broadcasting, including a video-marketing operation made redundant by the merger -- even though it employs one of Ted Turner's sons.
In addition, Atlantic Group, a recording division of Time Warner, Wednesday announced job cuts of as much as 13 percent of its 500-member staff.

The merger, proposed more than a year ago and reworked to meet the concerns of federal regulators about media industry concentration, was approved in separate shareholder meetings at the Time-Life Building in Manhattan.

At the podium, Turner wiped away tears as a Turner Broadcasting staffer of 22 years recounted the company's celebrated accomplishments, including the creation of Cable News Network and the World Series titles won by its Atlanta Braves baseball team.
"I really think this is the right thing to do for the company," Turner said, adding that the company's shares had hit an all-time high as the meeting closed.
Time Warner's stock closed up 25 cents at $41.375 on the New York Stock Exchange, while Turner gained 25 cents at $31 on the American Stock Exchange after having been as high as $31.375.
